units.title: Plant Systems
units.intro:
**Growth** = irreversible increase in size; **development** = new organs (leaf, flower). Seeds may stay dormant until water, warmth and oxygen arrive.

**Plant hormones:** auxin (tip → elongate cells, phototropism), gibberellin (stem / germination), cytokinin (cell division), ethene (ripening), abscisic acid (dormancy / stomatal close in drought).

cards.title: 6.1.1 Growth and Development in Flowering Plants
body: In plants growing points are found at the tip of stems and roots.
In special circumstances the young (immature) cells of a root, stem or leaf may become active and divide to form a new root or a new shoot.
Leaves have limited growth which determines their size and shape.
Young cells in the leaf-bud divide repeatedly to give rise to the leaf tissue.

cards.title: 6.1.2 Seed Dormancy and Germination
body: Dormant seeds are seeds which remain viable (alive) though metabolically inactive and incapable of germination under the conditions normally favourable for the species.
In other words, the seed is “asleep”, waiting for the ideal conditions to awaken.
**Seed dormancy** is a mechanism that ensures the survival of the species.
Dormancy enables the plant to avoid periods of environmental stress such as dry season or cold winter temperatures.

cards.title: 6.1.3 Plant Growth Hormones
body: Plant hormones are chemical substances that affect a plant’s ability to respond to its environment.
Plant hormones are also known as plant growth regulators because they can stimulate or inhibit plant growth.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: What is the primary physical process that initiates seed germination by causing the dry seed to absorb water passively?
cards.why:
**Step 1: Understand early germination stages**
Before cellular metabolism can begin, a dry seed must absorb water to activate cellular enzymes.

**Step 2: Identify the passive absorption process**
This passive absorption of water through the micropyle, which swells the cotyledons and bursts the seed coat, is called imbibition.

**Step 3: Final Result**
Therefore, the correct choice is **Imbibition**.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: Which plant hormone is responsible for cell elongation, phototrophic bending, and maintaining apical dominance?
cards.why:
**Step 1: Review phytohormone primary functions**
Gibberellins stimulate stem growth. ABA inhibits growth. Ethylene ripens fruit.

**Step 2: Identify auxin specific actions**
Auxin (primarily Indoleacetic acid, or $$IAA$$) regulates apical dominance, cell elongation, and phototropic curvature.

**Step 3: Final Result**
Therefore, the correct choice is **Auxin (IAA)**.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: Growth in plants growing points are found at the ______.
cards.why:
**Step 1:** Identify growing points (meristems). In plants, primary growth occurs at apical meristems.
**Step 2:** Locate apical meristems. These are found at the **tips of stems** (shoot apical meristem) and the **tips of roots** (root apical meristem).
**Step 3:** Select the option that includes both. Option D (B & C).

cards.title: 6.2 Plant Tissues
body: Plant cells are formed at meristems, and then develop into cell types which are grouped into tissues and tissue systems.
Plants have only three tissue systems, namely the dermal tissue system, ground tissue system and vascular tissue system.
Dermal tissue covers the outer surface of herbaceous plants.
Ground tissue comprises the bulk of the primary plant body.
Vascular tissue includes xylem, phloem, parenchyma and cambium cells.

lessons.title: The Root: Primary Structure and Function

cards.title: Tissues
body: Meristem (divides), parenchyma (pack), collenchyma / sclerenchyma (support), xylem (water up, dead tubes), phloem (sugar both ways, living).

cards.title: Root hair zone drinks; stem holds xylem/phloem; leaf is the factory; flower is the sex kit.
Tissues
body: Root systems: tap (one main, e.g. carrot) vs fibrous (grass). Regions: cap, division, elongation, hair/maturation. Leaf: cuticle, upper epidermis, palisade (photosynthesis), spongy + stomata (gas).

cards.title: 6.3.1 Tap and Fibrous Root Systems
body: The two principal functions of roots are the absorption of water and minerals, and anchorage.
When the seed germinates, the radicle is usually the first structure to appear; it becomes the first root and is called the **primary root**.
In many plants (e.g. beet, radish and carrot), the primary root remains the principal root throughout the life of the plant.
The development of a fibrous root system (like that of barley or wheat) is different from that of a tap root system.

cards.title: 6.3.2 Root Growth Regions
body: Root Cap: The root cap is made up of parenchyma cells that form an inverted cup-shape, as a covering for the tip of each root.
The outer part of the root cap is rough and uneven because its cells are constantly being worn away as the root pushes through the soil.
The main function of the root cap is to protect the delicate root tip.
The growing point also gives rise to new root cap cells to replace the ones that have worn away.

cards.title: 6.3.3 Internal Structure of the Root
body: In cross section, a root has an epidermis, cortex, endodermis and pericycle, and xylem and phloem.
**The cortex** is the tissue immediately inside the epidermis and functions in storing food.
The innermost layer of the cortex is the endodermis.
Inside the endodermis is a cylinder of parenchyma cells called the pericycle.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: What is the primary function of Abscisic Acid (ABA) in plants during environmental stress?

options.A: To promote rapid stem elongation and leaf growth
options.B: To accelerate fruit ripening and flower opening
options.C: To maintain seed dormancy and trigger rapid stomatal closure during water deficit
options.D: To stimulate cell division in lateral buds

cards.why:
**Step 1: Define ABA as a stress hormone**
$$ABA$$ is synthesized in plastids and acts as a key stress signaler.

**Step 2: Connect with water conservation**
Under drought stress, $$ABA$$ causes potassium ions to exit guard cells, closing stomata to prevent transpiration water loss, and maintains seed dormancy.

**Step 3: Final Result**
Therefore, the correct choice is **To maintain seed dormancy and trigger rapid stomatal closure during water deficit**.

lessons.title: The Shoot: Primary Structure and Function

cards.title: 6.4.1 The Stem: Structure and Function
body: The growing tip is protected by a number of overlapping young leaves which form the terminal bud.
The leaves are arranged in various ways on and around the axis.
The leaf arrangement can be described as alternate, opposite or, if they are found in groups of three or more, they are referred to as **whorled**.
The regions where the leaves attach to the stem are called **nodes**.

cards.title: 6.4.2 The Leaf: Structure and Function
body: **The leaf** is the site of food production in plants.
Leaves vary greatly in form and internal structure.
Monocots and dicots are distinguished on the basis of leaf structure.
Monocots have typically simple leaves with parallel venation, while dicots have branching venation.

cards.title: 6.4.3 The Flower: Structure and Function
body: **The flower** is the part of the shoot system specially modified for reproduction.
In a typical flower there are four sets of floral parts arranged in rings or whorls.
From the outside of the flower towards the centre, the four sets of floral parts are distinguished as the calyx, corolla, gynoecium and androecium.
Calyx: This is the outermost whorl, consisting of sepals.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: Which single layer of cells in the root cross-section contains the waterproof Casparian strip that regulates mineral entry?
cards.why:
**Step 1: Identify root vascular layers**
Water absorbed by roots passes through the epidermis and cortex toward the vascular cylinder.

**Step 2: Identify the regulatory barrier**
The endodermis is the innermost cortical layer. Its cell walls contain suberin (the Casparian strip), which blocks apoplastic water flow, forcing water to pass through cell membranes to regulate mineral entry.

**Step 3: Final Result**
Therefore, the correct choice is **Endodermis**.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: Which leaf mesophyll layer consists of tightly packed, vertically elongated cells optimized for capturing sunlight for photosynthesis?
cards.why:
**Step 1: Analyze leaf internal anatomy**
The leaf interior (mesophyll) is divided into palisade and spongy layers.

**Step 2: Match with photosynthetic specialization**
The palisade mesophyll is located on the upper surface, consisting of tightly packed, columnar cells rich in chloroplasts to maximize solar energy capture.

**Step 3: Final Result**
Therefore, the correct choice is **Palisade mesophyll**.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: In between upper and lower epidermis of the leaf section, there are palisade layer and spongy layer, both collectively known as____.
cards.why:
**Step 1:** Identify leaf layers. A typical leaf has a protective outer epidermis.
**Step 2:** Identify the internal tissue. The ground tissue located between the two epidermal layers is called the **mesophyll**.
**Step 3:** Sub-divide the mesophyll. It is usually differentiated into the **palisade mesophyll** (column-like cells for photosynthesis) and **spongy mesophyll** (loose cells for gas exchange).
**Step 4:** Conclusion. Collectively, they form the mesophyll layer.

cards.title: 6.5 Transport Systems in Plants
body: Soil water is absorbed by the root hairs.
Once the water enters a root hair it passes from one cell to another by osmosis until it reaches the xylem.
Water in the xylem moves up from the roots to the stem and leaves by the action of root pressure and transpiration pull.
Root pressure is one of the forces that push water up the xylem.
The pulling force set up by the evaporation of water from the leaves is called **transpiration pull**.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: Which of the following describes the double fertilization event in angiosperms?

options.A: Two sperm cells fertilize two separate egg cells to produce fraternal twins.
options.B: One sperm fertilizes the egg to form a zygote, while the second sperm fuses with two polar nuclei to form the triploid endosperm.
options.C: One sperm fertilizes the ovary wall, while the second sperm forms the seed coat.
options.D: Two pollen tubes fertilize the same egg to produce a diploid endosperm.

cards.why:
**Step 1: Review angiosperm reproductive events**
Angiosperms undergo a unique double fertilization process utilizing two sperm nuclei from a single pollen tube.

**Step 2: Trace both fertilization pathways**
One sperm ($$n$$) fertilizes the egg ($$n$$) to form a zygote ($$2n$$). The second sperm ($$n$$) fuses with the two polar nuclei ($$n+n$$) to form the triploid endosperm ($$3n$$).

**Step 3: Final Result**
Therefore, the correct choice is **One sperm fertilizes the egg to form a zygote, while the second sperm fuses with two polar nuclei to form the triploid endosperm.**

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: Which theory explains the upward transport of water through xylem vessels based on transpiration pull, molecular attraction, and water tension?
cards.why:
**Step 1: Review water transport models**
Water moves up tall plants under negative pressure (tension).

**Step 2: Name the primary model**
The cohesion-tension theory explains that water is pulled up by transpiration, held together by hydrogen bonds (cohesion), and supported by xylem walls (adhesion).

**Step 3: Final Result**
Therefore, the correct choice is **Cohesion-tension theory**.

cards.q: Sugars made in the leaves are carried to other parts of the plant through the ____.
cards.why:
**Step 1:** Xylem carries water and minerals upward from the roots.

**Step 2:** Phloem carries dissolved sugars (translocation) from leaves to roots, fruits and growing points.

**Step 3:** So sugars move in the phloem.

questions.q: Which of the following is a simple plant tissue?
why: **Simple tissues** are composed of only one type of cell. Examples include **Parenchyma**, Collenchyma, and Sclerenchyma. Xylem and Phloem are **complex tissues** because they consist of multiple cell types.

questions.q: The absorption of water by seeds is known as_______.
why:
**Step 1:** Define the terms.
- Transpiration: Loss of water vapor from leaves.
- Micropyle: Small opening in the seed coat.
- **Imbibition:** The physical process of water absorption by dry seeds, which causes them to swell and triggers germination.
questions.tip: Read every option before choosing; rule out the ones that contradict the notes.

questions.q: All of the following are correct, except

options.A: abscisic acid are inhibits other hormones
options.B: cytokinins promote cell division in plants
options.C: ethylene is responsible for the ripening of fruit
options.D: auxins influence the stimulation of seed germination

why:
**Step 1:** Review plant hormone functions.
- A is correct: ABA is a stress hormone and growth inhibitor.
- B is correct: Cytokinins promote cytokinesis (cell division).
- C is correct: Ethylene gas triggers fruit ripening.
**Step 2:** Evaluate D. While auxins influence many growth processes, **Gibberellins** are the primary hormones responsible for stimulating seed germination. High levels of auxins can actually inhibit germination in some cases.

why: The micropyle is a tiny pore in the seed coat (testa). Its primary function is to allow water to enter the seed to initiate germination (imbibition).

questions.q: Which of the following is true about inhibitors in seed dormancy?

options.C: they are found in food storage tissue
options.D: they are found in outer covering of the seed or fruit

why:
**Step 1:** Understand seed dormancy. Dormancy is a state that prevents seeds from germinating even under favorable conditions.
**Step 2:** Identify chemical inhibitors. Hormones like Abscisic Acid (ABA) act as inhibitors.
**Step 3:** Locate these inhibitors. They can be found in various parts of the seed or fruit, including the endosperm, cotyledons, storage tissues, and the seed coat (outer covering) to prevent premature germination.
questions.tip: Read every option before choosing; rule out the ones that contradict the notes.

questions.q: Which of the following hormone is responsible for ripening of fruits?
why:
**Logic:**
- **Cytokinin:** Cell division.
- **Auxin:** Cell elongation.
- **Ethylene:** A gaseous hormone that triggers **fruit ripening** and leaf fall.
- **Gibberellin:** Stem growth.
- **Abscisic Acid:** Inhibits growth (stress hormone).

**Result:**
Ethylene.
questions.tip: Read every option before choosing; rule out the ones that contradict the notes.

questions.q: Meristematic tissues are

options.A: are absent on the tips of a stem.
options.B: are absent on the tips of a root.
options.C: have no capacity of continuous division.
options.D: are absent on the tips of leaves.

why: **Meristematic tissues** are specialized for continuous cell division and are found at the growing tips of roots and stems (apical meristems). They are generally not found at the tips of leaves, making D the correct factual statement among the choices.

questions.q: A group of plants with out specialized vascular cells are ______?
why:
**Step 1: Define vascular plants.**
Vascular plants have xylem and phloem to transport water and nutrients.

**Step 2: Categorize the options.**
- **Ferns, Pines, Beans:** All are vascular plants.
- **Mosses (Bryophytes):** Non-vascular plants that lack specialized conducting tissues.

questions.q: Identify the plant hormone that initiates the conversion of starch in fruits into sugar?
why: Ethylene is the gaseous plant hormone responsible for fruit ripening. During ripening, it triggers enzymes that break down complex starches into simple sugars, making the fruit sweet.

questions.q: Seed germination normally does not depend on
why: Seed germination requires water (to soften the seed coat), oxygen (for aerobic respiration to provide energy), and a suitable temperature. **Carbon dioxide** is needed for photosynthesis, but since a germinating seed hasn't grown leaves yet, it doesn't need CO2 to start growing.
